records.sourceFile: Repetitive Head Impacts in Youth    Football- Description and Relationship to White Matter Structure.pdf

paper.citation: Nilsson KJ, Flint HG, Gao Y, Kendrick L, Cutchin S, Pentecost R, et al. Repetitive Head Impacts in Youth Football: Description and Relationship to White Matter Structure. Sports Health. 2019.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort study compared diffusion tensor imaging fractional anisotropy (FA) before and after a season in 8-12 year old males in youth tackle football (35) and age-matched swimmers (12). Head impacts were recorded with helmet-mounted accelerometers in the football group, and the study tested whether impact number, magnitude or location correlated with FA change.
paper.tldr: In this small pilot study, one season of youth tackle football did not change white matter FA compared with swimmers. Higher total lateral head-impact magnitude was linked to increased left cingulate FA, but its meaning is unclear.
paper.methods: Males aged 8-12 in tackle football (35) and swimming (12) had 3T brain MRI with DTI before and after the season. Football players wore Shockbox accelerometers that recorded 1,905 impacts over the season, and FA was measured in manually placed regions of interest. A mixed-model repeated-measures MANOVA compared groups, and correlation and regression linked impact measures to FA change.
paper.findings: There was no group-by-time interaction for FA, and no pre-to-post change within the football group. Impacts were 17.9% in games and 82.1% in practices, with 301 impacts of 80 g or more. Total magnitude of lateral impacts correlated with increased left cingulate FA (r = 0.40, p = 0.03; regression beta 0.028).
paper.limitations: The study was a pilot with no sample-size estimate, so non-significant results are uninformative. The accelerometers did not record impacts below 30 g or rotational acceleration, and parents reported some data. The text gives 35 football players in one place and 34 in the hit data, and five MRI scans were excluded.
paper.practicalImplications: Practices produced most recorded head impacts because there were far more practices than games (31 vs 7), while the impact rate per session was similar (1.5 per game and per practice). Accelerometer counts of high-magnitude impacts should be interpreted cautiously, since this cohort's share of impacts of 80 g or more was far higher than in prior youth studies. Do not use the cingulate FA correlation to judge an individual athlete's brain health or injury risk, since the study does not show whether it is harmful.
paper.athleteDev: This study has no performance outcomes. For performance staff, its only use is to show how head-impact exposure accumulated across practices and games in one youth season. It should not be used to judge cognition, readiness or athlete development.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It has no return-to-play, symptom or recovery outcomes, and its imaging findings should not be used to clear or hold an athlete.

records.sourceFile: Static and Dynamic Cognitive Performance in Youth and Collegiate Athletes With Concussion.pdf

paper.citation: Brilliant AN, Meehan WP III, Howell DR. Static and Dynamic Cognitive Performance in Youth and Collegiate Athletes With Concussion. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared cognitive task performance while standing still and while walking in youth and collegiate athletes with concussion and uninjured controls. Concussed athletes were tested within 10 days of injury, and the primary outcomes were accuracy and the number of task items completed.
paper.tldr: Athletes with a recent concussion answered fewer cognitive items while standing and walking, and were less accurate on two tasks only while walking. Dual-task testing may help show post-concussion deficits, but it has not been validated as a diagnostic test.
paper.methods: Ninety-four athletes with concussion (tested a mean of 5.1 days after injury while still symptomatic) and 97 uninjured controls, aged 8-21, completed three cognitive tasks (backward spelling, serial subtraction and reverse months) in a 30-second standing condition and while walking 8 m. Accuracy and completion rate were compared with ANCOVA adjusted for sex, height and concussion history, and gait speed and symptoms were also measured.
paper.findings: Concussed athletes completed fewer responses while standing (37.3 vs 45.1, p = 0.03) and while walking (22.7 vs 33.6, p < 0.001). Overall accuracy did not differ while standing (p = 0.11) or walking (p = 0.15), but while walking they were less accurate on backward spelling (81.2% vs 89.8%, p = 0.049) and reverse months (95.8% vs 98.2%, p = 0.031). Concussed athletes also walked more slowly in both single-task and dual-task conditions and reported more symptoms.
paper.limitations: This was a single cross-sectional test, with no recovery follow-up and no test of diagnostic accuracy, and recruitment came from one clinic and one university. The standing task was always done before the walking task in a fixed order, and the per-task accuracy differences were borderline with several comparisons. The abstract gives p = 0.034 for reverse months while Table 3 gives p = 0.031; the table value is used here. Concussed athletes had more prior concussions (64% vs 27%) and were shorter, which was handled with covariates, but residual confounding is possible.
paper.practicalImplications: Within about 10 days of a concussion, a brief walking-plus-cognitive task may show slower responses and some accuracy loss, so it can be a useful adjunct to the full evaluation. Record the number of responses as well as accuracy, since the response count showed the most consistent group difference. Do not use these scores alone to clear an athlete or to rule a concussion in or out.
paper.athleteDev: This study has no performance or development outcomes. Its relevance for performance staff is limited to the idea that cognitive performance under movement may be a useful adjunct measure after concussion, not a training or readiness metric for healthy athletes.
paper.rtp: This study cannot establish when an athlete is ready to return to sport. It tested athletes while still symptomatic within 10 days of injury and did not follow recovery; the authors suggest the method may help assess readiness, but that was not tested.

records.sourceFile: Smooth Pursuit Velocity After a Season of Repetitive Head Impacts in American Football Players.pdf

paper.citation: Murray NG, Fenner M, Szekely B, Quigley KG, Islas A, Cipriani D, et al. Smooth Pursuit Velocity After a Season of Repetitive Head Impacts in American Football Players. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2025.
paper.abstract: This single-center cohort study measured smooth pursuit eye movement velocity with a Landolt-C eye-tracking task at preseason, midseason and postseason in 25 male Division I football players and 10 noncontact controls. Football players were grouped as high-dose or low-dose by instrumented mouthguard head-impact totals, and the study tested whether impacts were associated with smooth pursuit velocity across one season.
paper.tldr: Smooth pursuit eye velocity did not fall over one football season, and it was not linked to head-impact totals. Players later classed as high-dose were already slower than controls before the season, which the authors suggest may reflect prior contact history.
paper.methods: Players wore instrumented mouthguards that recorded impacts of 5 g or more, with a random sample of sessions video-verified, and completed eye tracking before contact practice, at midseason and within 2 weeks after the season. Players were split after the season into high-dose (above the 50th percentile on total impacts, peak linear and peak angular acceleration) and low-dose groups. Eye tracking used a Landolt-C target moving horizontally at 30 and 90 deg/s, and a mixed-model repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-corrected follow-ups and Pearson correlations were used.
paper.findings: Smooth pursuit velocity had a main effect of group but no time effect and no group-by-time interaction. Before the season, high-dose players were slower than controls (10.01 vs 15.60 deg/s), and at midseason both high-dose and low-dose players were slower than controls. No impact metric correlated with smooth pursuit velocity at any time point.
paper.limitations: The study was exploratory, from one team, with 25 players and 10 controls. Mouthguard data were missing for about 5 percent of impacts, controls were not matched for sex or sport and were tested over shorter intervals during their own terms, and only horizontal movements were measured. The text gives conflicting values for the preseason difference (4.28 in the abstract, 6.34 and 5.59 elsewhere) and gives 27 rather than 25 players in one place.
paper.practicalImplications: Eye-tracking values recorded before contact practices may already differ between high-exposure players and controls, so record a pre-season baseline if this measure is used. This study does not show that smooth pursuit tracks head-impact exposure during a season, so it should not be used alone to assess brain health or injury risk. Its finding of no seasonal decline supports only short-term stability in this small sample.
paper.athleteDev: Smooth pursuit velocity showed no seasonal decline and no link to head-impact totals in this study, so it is not a training or performance metric here. Its only practical value for performance staff is as a possible baseline measure, not as a readiness or development indicator.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Players were medically cleared at baseline, and the study has no concussion, symptom or return-to-play outcomes, so smooth pursuit values should not be used to clear or hold an athlete.

records.sourceFile: Age of First Exposure to Contact Sports Is Not Associated With Worse Later-In-Life Brain Health in a Cohort of Community-Dwelling Older Men.pdf

paper.citation: Jo J, Wong G, Williams KL, Davis PJ, Rigney GH, Zuckerman SL, et al. Age of First Exposure to Contact Sports Is Not Associated With Worse Later-In-Life Brain Health in a Cohort of Community-Dwelling Older Men. Clin J Sport Med. 2024:1-8.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 69 community-dwelling older men with contact sport histories compared those who first played before age 12 (n=24) with those who started at 12 or older (n=45). Early exposure was not associated with depression, anxiety, general health problems, motor symptoms or functional status. After adjusting for age, prior concussions and total years of contact sport, early exposure was linked to lower cognitive complaint and neurobehavioral symptom scores.
paper.tldr: In this small survey of older men, starting contact sport before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life brain health. The study cannot show that early play is beneficial, and the lower symptom scores in the early group should be read cautiously.
paper.methods: Men in a memory research registry completed an online or paper survey on age of first exposure to contact sport, sport history, concussion history, depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), general health, motor symptoms and functional status. Groups were compared with t tests and chi-square tests, and multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, prior concussions and total contact sport years.
paper.findings: Early exposure (before 12) was not associated with depression or anxiety scores in adjusted models. In adjusted models the early-exposure group had lower BC-CCI and NSI scores (standardized beta 0.29 for both, P=0.03), but the unadjusted differences for these two measures were not significant (P=0.065 and P=0.072), and the early group reported more total years of contact sport (10.8 vs 5.6, P=0.016).
paper.limitations: The sample is small (69 men, 24 in the early group), relies on self-report and recall, and was not verified with clinical or neuropsychological testing. The authors' clinical relevance statement that early benefits may outweigh head-impact risks goes beyond what a cross-sectional survey can show.
paper.practicalImplications: Based on this study alone, early contact sport participation should not be assumed to cause worse brain health in older men. Long-term benefit cannot be concluded from these data, and decisions about youth participation need evidence from prospective studies.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not measure athletic performance, skill development or training outcomes, so it cannot guide talent identification, sport selection or training decisions.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return to sport. The study surveyed older men years after their playing careers and did not assess concussed athletes, symptom recovery or return-to-play timing.

records.sourceFile: Sleep Architecture Immediately After a Sport-Related Concussion Sustained During a Professional Rugby Union Match - A Retrospective Case Study.pdf

paper.citation: Uchiyama K, Peeling P, Halson SL, Reid M, Wallman K, Walsh J, et al. Sleep Architecture Immediately After a Sport-Related Concussion Sustained During a Professional Rugby Union Match: A Retrospective Case Study. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2025 (ahead of print).
paper.abstract: This retrospective case study describes sleep architecture and overnight physiology in one professional rugby union player across four nights: before injury, the night of a concussion, the second night after injury with westward travel, and after recovery. On the night of injury, deep (N3) and REM sleep were reduced and total sleep was under 6 hours. The second night showed partial recovery of sleep stages but persistent fragmentation, lower oxygen saturation, higher heart rate, lower heart rate variability and more respiratory events.
paper.tldr: A single case showed that sleep became shorter and more fragmented, with less deep and REM sleep, on the night of a rugby concussion and remained disrupted the next night. Because this is one player with no repeated baselines, the findings suggest a pattern to test in larger studies rather than a settled effect.
paper.methods: Home-based polysomnography (Somfit) recorded sleep on one pre-injury night, the night of injury, the second night after injury and a night 24 days later. Sleep stages were manually scored in 30-second epochs, and heart rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate variability and respiratory events were extracted and analyzed descriptively against clinically meaningful thresholds.
paper.findings: On the night of injury, total sleep was 332 minutes (vs 261 pre-injury), with lower N3 (19%) and REM (18%) percentages than on all other nights. On the second night, sleep onset was 23 minutes, wake after sleep onset was 69 minutes, and sleep efficiency was below 85%. Mean heart rate was higher and heart rate variability was lower (65.1 and 66.9 ms vs 74.2 and 74.0 ms) on the injury and second nights than before and after injury, and respiratory events were higher (69 and 104 vs 14 pre-injury).
paper.limitations: The study is one player with a single pre-injury baseline night, so the apparent increase in sleep duration on the injury night probably reflects short sleep before injury rather than a concussion effect. Caffeine, alcohol and medication use were not recorded, and travel fatigue was not separated from concussion effects. The abstract says respiratory events were greater on the injury and second nights, but the results also report more events on the recovered night (46 vs 14).
paper.practicalImplications: In a concussed athlete, sleep quality may be poor for the first one to two nights, so staff could ask about sleep and monitor it in that window. Travel on the night after injury may add to sleep disruption, which is a reason to consider travel timing in the early phase. Routine sleep-apnea screening for collision athletes is a reasonable question to raise, but this case alone does not establish that it improves recovery.
paper.athleteDev: This study does not assess performance, training adaptation or skill, so it cannot guide training load or performance targets.
paper.rtp: The study can suggest that sleep should be checked in the first 72 hours after a concussion, but it cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that sleep disruption delays return to sport. It was one player with no symptom data reported, so it should not be used to time clearance.

records.sourceFile: Validity of research based on publicly obtained data in sports medicine - A quantitative assessment of concussions in the National Football League.pdf

paper.citation: Inclan PM, Kuhn AW, Chang PS, Mack C, Solomon GS, Sills AK, et al. Validity of Research Based on Publicly Obtained Data in Sports Medicine: A Quantitative Assessment of Concussions in the National Football League. Sports Health. 2023.
paper.abstract: This systematic review identified 20 NFL concussion studies that relied on publicly obtained internet data and compared the studies' counts with the NFL injury database for 2015 to 2019 where possible. The public-data studies captured about 70% of concussions on average, with a range of 20% to 90%. They over-represented running backs and quarterbacks and under-represented offensive linemen, defensive backs and linebackers, and misclassified special teams injuries.
paper.tldr: Concussion counts drawn from public internet sources captured on average about 70% of NFL concussions, with wide variation between studies. Public-data concussion research in the NFL should be read with caution, and curated league data are preferable.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-guided systematic search of medical and gray literature for NFL concussion studies that used publicly obtained data was completed in November 2020, and two reviewers independently screened and extracted data. Studies were compared with the NFL injury database (2015 to 2019) for capture rate, game phase distribution and position representation, using a relative representation ratio.
paper.findings: Of 20 included studies, 12 could be compared with NFL data, and they captured on average 70.0% (SD 25.0%) of concussions, with a range of 20.1% to 90.2%. Public-data studies reported 55% of concussions on offense, 45% on defense and under 1% on special teams, versus 44%, 37% and 18% in the NFL data. Running backs (ratio 1.46) and quarterbacks (1.42) were over-represented, and defensive backs (0.88), linebackers (0.82) and offensive linemen (0.93) were under-represented.
paper.limitations: The review depends on the NFL database as the reference standard, which the authors note still relies on clinical reporting across 32 teams, and several authors are NFL employees or consultants. Capture rates divide each study's annual count by NFL annual averages from 2015 to 2019, even though most included studies covered earlier seasons. None of the included studies described how concussions were diagnosed, and return-to-play outcomes were not analyzed.
paper.practicalImplications: Concussion counts or position-specific risks taken from public internet sources should not be used alone to estimate NFL injury risk, since they miss many injuries and over-represent high-profile positions. Staff who need reliable concussion data should prefer curated, clinically reported surveillance data where it can be obtained.
paper.athleteDev: This review addresses injury data quality and not performance measurement, so it cannot guide training or talent decisions. Performance statistics from public sources were not validated in this review.
paper.rtp: None of the included public-data studies described how concussions were diagnosed, and the review does not report return-to-play findings. It cannot be used to set or judge return-to-play timing for individual players.

records.sourceFile: Does reducing the height of the tackle through law change in elite men's rugby union reduce the incidence of concussion - A controlled study in 126 games.pdf

paper.citation: Stokes KA, Locke D, Roberts S, Henderson L, Tucker R, Ryan D, et al. Does reducing the height of the tackle through law change in elite men's rugby union (The Championship, England) reduce the incidence of concussion? A controlled study in 126 games. Br J Sports Med. 2019:1-6.
paper.abstract: This observational cohort study compared two competitions in English elite men's rugby during 2018/19, one played under standard tackle laws and one with the maximum tackle height lowered to the armpit line. The lowered tackle height reduced upright tackles and head and neck contact by ball carriers. Concussion incidence did not differ between the two settings, but tacklers were concussed more often under the lowered tackle height.
paper.tldr: Lowering the maximum tackle height in English elite rugby changed how players tackled, but it did not reduce overall concussion rates and tacklers were concussed more often. Law changes like this should be tested with larger, better-controlled studies before they are used to reduce concussion.
paper.methods: Video analysts coded 52 game and tackle variables for 126 matches, and injury and concussion data were collected by club medical staff using the standard head injury assessment protocol. Tackle behaviour and concussion incidence per 1000 hours and per 1000 tackles were compared between the standard-law Championship (90 matches) and the lowered-height Championship Cup (36 matches) using rate ratios.
paper.findings: Under the lowered height, tacklers made head and neck contact with ball carriers about 30% less often (RR 0.70), and tacklers were upright less often and fully bent more often. Overall concussion incidence was 16.9 per 1000 hours under standard laws and 22.2 under lowered height (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.85 to 2.01, not significant). Tacklers had higher concussion incidence (6.9 vs 13.2 per 1000 hours, RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.45).
paper.limitations: The two periods were different competitions, so differences in squad selection, match importance and season timing may explain the results. Concussion rates were 20% higher in the post-law period under standard laws, which may reflect better reporting because of the study, and two rounds with unusually high or low counts influenced the comparison. Data were available for 86% of players, and the study was not powered for concussion outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Lowering the tackle height changed tackle technique but did not reduce concussion in this study, and tacklers had a higher concussion incidence and propensity under the lowered height. Medical and coaching staff should not assume that a tackle-height law change will reduce concussion without monitoring outcomes in their own competition.
paper.athleteDev: This study addresses tackle behaviour and injury risk rather than performance, so it cannot guide performance targets. Under the lowered height, tacklers entered contact fully bent more often and made more passive shoulder and arm tackles, which describes how technique shifted but not whether it is safer to coach.
paper.rtp: The study does not address return to play, symptom recovery or clearance after concussion, so it cannot be used to set return-to-play timing. Its concussion counts describe incidence only.

records.sourceFile: The importance of language in describing concussions - A qualitative analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Knowles P, Schneider K, Bugwadia AK, Sorcar P, Pea RD, Daneshvar DH, et al. The importance of language in describing concussions: A qualitative analysis. PM&R. 2024:1-8.
paper.abstract: This secondary qualitative analysis of 94 phone interviews with high school sports stakeholders examined whether people who rated concussion as more severe were more likely to describe it using the word brain. The association was significant overall and among coaches, but not among athletes, parents, educators or the athletic director. The authors conclude that precise medical language may support concussion education and reporting.
paper.tldr: People who saw concussion as more severe were more likely to describe it as a brain injury, and this was clearest among high school coaches. Concussion education for coaches may benefit from clear brain-injury language, although this study did not measure reporting.
paper.methods: Semistructured telephone interviews were conducted in July 2017 with 94 participants from a larger set of 316, selected because one interviewer asked the same questions and the interviews were recorded. Two coders assigned each participant to a minimum, moderate or maximum severity category based on how they ranked concussion among common injuries, and recorded whether they used brain language. Chi-square tests, Fisher's exact tests and odds ratios were used for the analysis.
paper.findings: Brain language was used by 1 of 19 minimum-severity participants (5%), 10 of 43 moderate (23%) and 18 of 32 maximum (56%), P<.001 overall. With maximum severity as the reference, the odds of using brain terms were lower in the minimum (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.30) and moderate (OR 0.24, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.65) groups. The association held for coaches (P=.002; OR 0.06 and 0.14 versus maximum) but not for parents, athletes or educators (all P>.05).
paper.limitations: The sample came from convenience recruitment, mostly through cold emails and LinkedIn, and some participants were known to the interviewer, which may have influenced responses. Severity was coded from open-ended answers that could mean pain, time out or long-term effect. The subgroup analyses were small, and the authors note that the non-coach results may reflect low power rather than no relationship.
paper.practicalImplications: Concussion education for coaches could describe concussion explicitly as a brain injury, which is consistent with the link between brain language and perceived severity seen here. The study shows an association only and did not measure reporting, so staff should not expect that changing wording alone will change how often athletes report concussions.
paper.athleteDev: This study is about how people describe and rate concussion severity and does not address performance, training or skill development, so it cannot guide performance decisions.
paper.rtp: The study records attitudes about whether an athlete would return to the game after a concussion, but it did not measure return-to-play decisions or outcomes. It should not be used to set return-to-play criteria or timing.

records.sourceFile: Neurocognitive Deficits Associated                        With ADHD in Athletes- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Poysophon P, Rao AL. Neurocognitive Deficits Associated With ADHD in Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Health. 2018.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 17 studies examined whether athletes with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have more neurocognitive deficits, concussion risk, symptom reporting and slower recovery. Athletes with ADHD generally scored lower on neurocognitive testing, reported more symptoms, and in several studies had higher concussion risk. Evidence that stimulant medication changes these risks was sparse.
paper.tldr: Athletes with ADHD in these studies tended to score lower on neurocognitive testing and report more concussion-like symptoms, and several studies found higher concussion rates. Many differences were small and the stimulant evidence is limited, so ADHD history should be used as context rather than as a diagnostic or return-to-play decision.
paper.methods: PubMed, CINAHL, PsychInfo and Cochrane were searched for studies of athletes aged 15 to 19 with ADHD that used neuropsychological testing, with 17 studies meeting criteria from the 2013 to 2017 literature. Findings were grouped by study type, sample size and effect size and synthesized qualitatively, because the data were too variable for quantitative analysis.
paper.findings: Athletes with ADHD had lower ImPACT composite scores in several studies, with differences of 0.01 to 6 points that the authors describe as small and within the normative range for adolescents. Six mostly cross-sectional studies found more frequent prior concussion in athletes with ADHD (for example, 1 or more prior concussions in 50.4% vs 14.4% in one study), while two found no difference. Stimulant-treated athletes had worse verbal and visual memory and higher symptom scores than controls in one study, and the evidence on stimulants was limited and conflicting.
paper.limitations: The authors note that ADHD diagnoses were self-reported or from charts without clinical confirmation, stimulant use was self-reported, only two studies were prospective, and confounders were inconsistently controlled. The abstract states that there was no evidence that stimulant treatment changed these risks, but the text reports one study (Iverson et al) where stimulant use was associated with a higher concussion risk. The abstract gives a prevalence range of 4.2% to 8.1%, while the discussion gives 4% to 14.3%.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes with a known ADHD history may have lower baseline test scores and higher self-reported symptoms, so staff should interpret baseline and post-concussion testing with that history in mind and not treat it as a diagnosis. This review does not support a conclusion on whether stimulant medication is safe or effective in athletes, so medication decisions should involve the treating clinician and not be based on this review alone.
paper.athleteDev: This review does not address performance or training outcomes, so it cannot guide talent identification or training decisions.
paper.rtp: The review reports ImPACT scores and symptoms relevant to concussion, but it does not establish return-to-play criteria. Its finding of longer recovery is based on one small study that was not statistically significant, so it should not be used to set return-to-play timing for athletes with ADHD.

records.sourceFile: Role of advanced neuroimaging,      fluid biomarkers and genetic testing in the assessment of sport-related      concussion- a systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: McCrea M, Meier T, Huber D, Ptito A, Bigler E, Debert CT, et al. Role of advanced neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers and genetic testing in the assessment of sport-related concussion: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2017 (published online April 28, 2017).
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 98 studies assessed advanced neuroimaging, fluid biomarkers and genetic testing in sport-related concussion. Neuroimaging, biomarker and genetic studies all showed concussion-related effects, but the authors rated the evidence for clinical use as low in each area. They conclude that these methods are promising research tools that need further validation before clinical use.
paper.tldr: Advanced brain imaging, blood biomarkers and genetic tests showed concussion-related changes in research studies, but none is ready for routine clinical use. These methods should be treated as research tools and not as diagnostic or return-to-play measures.
paper.methods: Three separate systematic searches of Medline, PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Scopus and Cochrane covered neuroimaging, biomarkers and genetics in sport-related concussion, from January 2000 to December 2016. Two reviewers screened articles, risk of bias was rated with a modified QUADAS-2 tool, and the level of evidence was graded with a modified GRADE approach. Findings were summarized in tables and narrative synthesis.
paper.findings: Across 76 neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies (DTI 18, task fMRI 15, EEG/qEEG 16, MRS 13, resting-state fMRI 8, and fewer using other methods), each modality showed significant concussion-related effects, although directions varied between studies and some reported null results. Eleven of 16 fluid biomarker studies found significant changes in blood markers such as S100B, total tau and AMPAR, while markers including NSE, VILIP-1 and salivary cortisol did not distinguish concussed athletes. The six genetic studies were small and provided proof of concept only, for example a GRIN2A variant associated with recovery times over 60 days.
paper.limitations: The review notes high or moderate risk of bias in most studies, driven by limited generalizability (male-only, collegiate, or single-sport samples), small samples, lack of preinjury baselines, inconsistent definitions of concussion, and publication bias. The authors also note that the review was broad by design and included few studies per marker, so the evidence for individual markers is thin.
paper.practicalImplications: Advanced neuroimaging, blood biomarkers and genetic testing should not be used for routine concussion diagnosis or management based on this review. Staff interested in these tools should look for studies with preinjury baselines, standardized protocols and clinically relevant outcomes before considering their use.
paper.athleteDev: This review concerns concussion assessment and biology and does not address performance measurement or training, so it cannot guide performance decisions.
paper.rtp: The authors state that these markers are not validated for clinical decisions, including when an athlete is fit to return to activity. The review cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or timing, though it suggests future studies may link biomarkers to recovery.
